title: Exploring Bivariate Numerical Data: Visual Guide
outline: Title: Exploring Bivariate Numerical Data: Visual Guide

1. Table To Scatterplot | the same rows shown as a two-way table of counts and as a cloud of points, with a pattern selector, a spread dial and an optional far-off observation | two quantitative variables need one point per paired observation, and the direction, strength and outlier verdict is read off the points themselves rather than off the button that made them

2. Trend Line And Prediction | a draggable slope and intercept over eleven points, with the gaps above and below counted and a prediction marker that crosses out of the observed x-range | a trend line summarises the pattern by balancing the gaps rather than touching the points, and predicting outside the observed range is an assumption the data cannot support

3. Correlation Versus Slope | a dial that sets r exactly, quadrant marks showing which points push r up or down, and a units toggle that multiplies y by five | r is an average of z-score products so it is unitless and bounded by -1 and 1, while the slope carries units and changes with them: b = r times s_y over s_x

4. Minimizing Squared Residuals | nine points with a literal square drawn on every residual, a slope dial, and the total of those squares plotted against the slope | the least-squares line is defined by minimising the sum of squared residuals, it always passes through the point of averages, and its slope is exactly r times s_y over s_x

5. Residuals And One Outlier | a movable loose observation with the line fitted both with and without it, the residual plot underneath, and a switch to curved underlying data | residual is observed minus predicted, a curved residual plot means a nonlinear model may fit better, and one influential point can pull the line and change r and r-squared
